summary: Describes a way to forward media access control frames over MAPOS, the Multiple Access Protocol over SONET/SDH. The aim is to let a MAPOS network and traditional MAC-based local area networks work together as one environment. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Two kinds of networks speak slightly different languages. This note explains how to wrap messages from one so they can ride across the other.

questions: how to forward mac frames over mapos
subtitle: Bridging local area networks through MAPOS optical networks.

tldr.problem: Distant local area networks (LANs) connected to different physical locations need to communicate transparently as if they were on the same network segment.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes how to encapsulate MAC (Media Access Control) frames inside MAPOS (Multiple Access Protocol over SONET/SDH) frames, allowing network adapters at each LAN to transparently forward frames across the MAPOS backbone while mapping MAC addresses to MAPOS addresses.
tldr.outcome: Geographically separated LANs can be unified into a single virtual LAN (VLAN) segment using a MAPOS-based metropolitan or wide-area backbone, providing a transparent LAN service.

facts.label: Maximum VLAN peer adapters per RFC

today: RFC 3422 is an Informational memo describing a practical MAPOS bridging technique deployed in the early 2000s. It has not been updated or obsoleted, but MAPOS itself has largely given way to more modern technologies like MPLS and Metro Ethernet. The technique remains valid for implementations that use MAPOS for carrier networks.

sections.title: The Problem: Distant Networks Need to Work Together
sections.content:
This RFC solves a practical networking problem: how to connect local area networks at different geographic locations as if they were physically adjacent, all part of the same LAN segment. Without a solution, a LAN at one office and a LAN at another would be separate islands of communication.

The method described here lets a MAPOS network—a switching backbone built on SONET/SDH optical fiber—act as a transparent bridge between distant LANs. A Network Adapter (NA) at each LAN handles the translation: it encapsulates outgoing MAC frames (the native format for Ethernet and similar networks) into MAPOS frames for transmission across the backbone, then unwraps incoming MAPOS frames back into MAC frames for the local LAN.
sections.plainLanguage: Two offices need to act like one office network-wise. The RFC explains how to package messages from one office's network so they survive the journey through the long-distance network and arrive at the other office in the right format.

sections.title: The Network Model: LANs, Adapters, and MAPOS
sections.content:
The setup has three main parts. MAC-based LANs (Ethernet switches and hosts at each location) speak the language of their local network. A Network Adapter (NA) sits at the boundary of each LAN with two faces: an Ethernet port connecting to the local LAN, and a MAPOS port connecting to the backbone. The MAPOS network in the middle consists of MAPOS switches connected by SONET/SDH leased lines and optical fiber cables.

Each Network Adapter gets a unique MAPOS address assigned by the NSP (Node-Switch Protocol). This address lets the MAPOS switches forward encapsulated frames from one NA to another. The result is a unified VLAN: hosts at one LAN can send frames to hosts at another as if they shared the same physical medium.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of post offices (network adapters) at two ends that know both local streets and the national mail system. They speak the local language inside the building but use mail trucks (MAPOS) to cross the distance.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Frame Forwarding
sections.content:
When a host in LAN N1 sends a MAC frame to a host in LAN N2, the following happens. The Network Adapter at N1 receives the frame on its Ethernet interface. It then encapsulates the frame: it prepends MAPOS headers (including the source MAPOS address of the sending NA and a destination MAPOS address) to the original MAC frame, creating a MAPOS frame. This bundled frame travels across the MAPOS network.

At the destination, the Network Adapter at N2 receives the MAPOS frame, strips off the MAPOS headers, and forwards the original MAC frame to its local LAN. To the hosts, the communication appears local—they see only MAC frames, unaware of the MAPOS wrapping that occurred.

The RFC specifies the exact format of the encapsulated frame for different MAC types (Ethernet, Token Ring, FDDI) and whether VLANs are tagged. The MAPOS header includes a protocol field set to 0xFE31 to identify bridged LAN traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The network adapter wraps the letter (MAC frame) in a special envelope marked for MAPOS delivery, sends it through the national system, and the receiving adapter removes the envelope so the letter looks local again.

sections.title: Finding the Destination: Address Mapping and Discovery
sections.content:
A key challenge is determining which Network Adapter should receive a frame intended for a given MAC address. Each NA maintains an address table mapping MAC addresses to MAPOS addresses. When forwarding a unicast frame, the NA looks up the destination MAC address in this table. If found, the corresponding MAPOS address tells the MAPOS network where to send the encapsulated frame. If not found, the frame is treated as a broadcast and sent to all peer NAs in the same VLAN.

The address table can be populated two ways. Static setup requires manual configuration of MAC-to-MAPOS address mappings before the VLAN is used; these entries are permanent and take precedence. Dynamic discovery learns entries automatically: when an NA receives an encapsulated frame with a source MAC address it has not seen before, it adds the source MAC address and the source MAPOS address to its table. These dynamic entries expire after a configurable timeout (default 300 seconds), allowing addresses to be recycled if a host moves.
sections.plainLanguage: The adapters keep a phone book: when a message arrives from a name they do not know, they write down where that name came from so they can reply. If they see the name again, they look it up; if not, they call everyone in the VLAN.

sections.title: Security and Access Control
sections.content:
The RFC acknowledges that a MAPOS VPN service crosses administrative boundaries. Carriers typically own the MAPOS network and optical lines, while customers own their LANs. The Network Adapters are the primary defense: they sit in customer premises but are controlled by the carrier, making them critical security points.

Key protections include frame filtering: each NA accepts only bridged MAPOS frames from known VLAN peer adapters (based on stored MAPOS addresses). Discovered address table entries are rejected if the MAPOS source address does not match a known peer. NAs can also monitor broadcast traffic from any host and drop frames from hosts that exceed a broadcast threshold, preventing denial-of-service attacks from a compromised or rogue device. MAPOS switches can filter at the network level, rejecting frames with source addresses that do not match what was assigned via NSP.

An authentication mechanism similar to CHAP (Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol) is suggested for future implementation to verify that a NA reconnecting to the MAPOS network is legitimate.
sections.plainLanguage: The adapters are like border guards who check that each message comes from a known peer before accepting it, and they watch for anyone trying to flood the system with too many messages.
